expectations.text: Does not simply validate the 10/10 split as best practice without substantive caveats
expectations.evidence: 'standard' and 'good' are two different things here, and this particular standard has a well-documented empirical problem you need to plan around before you collect a single response.

expectations.text: Warns that negatively-worded reverse-scored items frequently form a separate method factor in EFA/CFA, creating artificial multidimensionality
expectations.evidence: what you very often get is not one clean personality factor. You get two factors: the substantive construct you were trying to measure, and a method factor defined almost entirely by item wording direction.

expectations.text: Notes that this method factor can suggest more dimensions than actually exist in the construct
expectations.evidence: You'll conclude you measured a two-dimensional construct when you set out to measure one. Your factor count is now wrong, and any downstream analyses (subscale scoring, structural models) will be built on that error.

expectations.text: Mentions that reverse-coded items often show lower factor loadings, worse discrimination, or worse fit than positively-worded items
expectations.evidence: your reverse-coded items may have lower factor loadings, lower corrected item-total correlations, and higher residual variances than your positive items. They're doing worse measurement work, not better.

expectations.text: Suggests alternatives or recommends planning to test for and account for the method factor (e.g., adding a method factor in CFA)
expectations.evidence: Plan to test and model the method factor explicitly. In your CFA, specify a priori that negatively-worded items may share residual covariance (a method factor), and compare: (a) one-factor model, (b) one-factor model with a method factor for negatively-worded items, (c) two-factor model.

expectations.text: Does not describe reverse-scoring as a reliable or robust solution to acquiescence bias
expectations.evidence: The acquiescence-control benefit of reverse-keyed items is much smaller than traditionally assumed, while the method-factor cost is real and often substantial... the 10/10 split is a reflex from an older literature. The empirical record since the mid-1990s says it often creates more measurement problems than it solves.
